body.text: Attribution: Tanusha Tyagi, “The Data Convergence: Reviewing Competition Laws Through the Privacy Lens,” ORF Occasional Paper No. 576, Observer Research Foundation, October 2026.

Data is considered the new raw material for the digital economy, today acquiring a status comparable to traditional factors of production, such as capital and labour.[1] The digital economy is heavily dependent on data, as control over it not only drives innovation and market efficiency,[2] but also shapes how users are profiled, targeted, and influenced.[3] The speed at which artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated into all aspects of businesses has further increased this interdependence. AI systems thrive on vast, diverse datasets, turning personal data into a decisive competitive advantage.

Personal data refers to any information about a living person that can be used to identify them, such as email address and browsing history.[4] Such information is valuable because it reveals user preferences, and access to personal data allows platforms to increase user influence, engage in targeted advertising, and manipulate user behaviour.[5] Firms with greater access to such data can develop more refined algorithms, achieve higher performance, and reinforce their dominance, but this happens at the expense of user choice and privacy.[6] Accordingly, this analysis builds on the premise that privacy erosion in digital markets is not merely a collateral harm of data-driven business models, but a structural condition embedded as a core feature that shapes competitive outcomes, market entry, and user choice.

Scholars have posited that privacy is an individual’s ability to control the terms under which personal data is acquired and used. In a 1968 paper, American jurist Charles Fried noted that having control over personal data allows users to create the necessary context for relationships of respect, friendship, and trust.[7] Thus, privacy can be understood not only as an absence of information about an individual in the minds of others, but as the control one has over information about oneself.

However, in the digital economy, privacy is no longer viewed only as a matter of individual rights, but has also become a parameter of competition. When firms weaken privacy protections through extensive data collection, opaque consent mechanisms, or restrictive data policies, they are altering the competitive quality of the service being offered.[8] However, users typically do not consider privacy degradation a disincentive to purchase or use digital goods because they usually share their information to gain additional convenience through personalisation, including through targeted advertisements.[9] Importantly, although users frequently accept such trade-offs, acceptance does not equate to meaningful choice.[10]

Privacy erosion is thus best understood not merely as a characteristic of digital services, but also as an avenue to exercise market power through competition enforcement. Jurisdictions in different parts of the world use privacy as a factor in determining whether competition has been harmed when enforcing competition rules.[11]

India’s competition regime has evolved from a control-oriented framework to one that addresses the complexities of data-driven markets. In 2002, India enacted the Competition Act,[12] based on the recommendations of the Raghavan Committee (2000),[13] which replaced the 1969 Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act.[14] While the Competition Act’s early focus lay in promoting user welfare, ensuring fair competition, and curbing abuse of dominance, this initial design reflected an analogue economy in which market power was assessed through price, output, and structural indicators rather than through data, algorithms, or network effects. The 2007 amendment,[15] which operationalised the Act and established the Competition Commission of India (CCI) as the key enforcement authority, laid the foundation for an independent regulator but did not yet anticipate the unique challenges of digital ecosystems.

As digital markets became central to economic growth, it became evident that traditional competition tools were inadequate to address the dominance of large online platforms. Recognising this, in 2019, the Competition Law Review Committee (CLRC) undertook a comprehensive assessment of the existing legal framework,[16] and acknowledged data as a relevant factor of consideration in zero-price markets.[17] The CLRC recognised that a price of zero does not mean consumers receive services without giving anything in return; instead, they contribute valuable personal data with every search, click, and interaction. However, the CLRC stopped short of recommending an ex-ante regulatory regime. This approach was further reflected in the CCI’s ‘Market Study on the Telecom Sector in India’ (2021),[18] which acknowledged that privacy could function as a non-price parameter of competition in digital markets.

Subsequently, the ‘Fifty-Third Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance’ (2022)[19] first flagged concerns about anti-competitive practices by Big Tech, identifying issues such as self-preferencing and exclusive dealing, among others. Building upon these observations, the ‘Sixtieth Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance’ (2023) reiterated that an ex-post enforcement model is insufficient in digital markets where dominance can tip irreversibly before regulatory intervention.[20] The report highlighted data accumulation as a competitive asset, noting that platforms that have collected a wealth of personal data over time will always have a competitive advantage over newer platforms in terms of their services.[21] It also recommended the adoption of a Digital Competition Law to introduce ex-ante obligations for “Systemically Significant Digital Enterprises (SSDEs),” since the market tips in favour of a dominant player in a short span of time—this may result in investigations by authorities that take place only after other competitors have already been pushed out of the market, i.e., ex-post regimes, which is not effective due to the time-consuming nature of enforcement proceedings.[22]

In 2023, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs constituted the Committee on Digital Competition Law to design a new legislative framework addressing the unique characteristics of digital markets. In February 2024, the committee presented the Draft Digital Competition Bill, which sought to regulate platform conduct proactively, imposing obligations related to data combination, preferential treatment, and user consent.[23] However, the standing committee in its 25th Report withdrew the Bill in August.[24] The committee said the Bill’s framework had rigid ex-ante obligations that could result in unnecessary burden on digital platforms without proper market analysis; it could also stifle innovation, deter foreign investment, and impose higher compliance costs on startups and MSMEs.[25]

Despite the Bill’s withdrawal, questions remain: How can market power in digital markets be identified and assessed within Indian competition law? The DCB’s intention to regulate platforms through the ex-ante designation of SSDEs marked a move away from the traditional definition of ‘dominance’ as used in Indian law. To evaluate whether this shift from an ‘effects-based’ definition of dominance is justified or whether the DCB’s withdrawal creates a regulatory gap, it is necessary to understand what Indian competition law has traditionally considered as ‘dominance’ and how this translates into data markets.

Under Section 4 of the 2002 Competition Act,[26] read alongside Section 19(4),[27] dominance is not determined through rigid thresholds but is assessed on a case-by-case basis.[28] The Act adopts a flexible framework, requiring the CCI to consider a range of non-exhaustive factors—including an enterprise’s market share, size, and resources, as well as barriers to entry, countervailing buyer power, and market structure—to determine whether an enterprise enjoys a position of strength that enables it to operate independently of competitive forces, or influence competitors, consumers, or the market in its favour. The 2023 Competition (Amendment) Act retains this approach, reflecting the legislature's preference for assessing impact over rigid classification. In its May 2025 ruling in Competition Commission of India vs Schott Glass India Pvt. Ltd.,[29] the Supreme Court also reaffirmed this position by mandating an effects-based analysis in cases related to the abuse of dominance under the 2002 Competition Act, stressing the importance of credible evidence of actual or likely harm to the competition over any presumptions or assumptions.

However, digital markets have created new forms of market power that the traditional understanding of dominance does not always capture. A company may gain a strong position not only because of its size or pricing strategies but also because it can collect, combine, and use large amounts of personal and non-personal data, giving it an advantage over its competitors.[30] This distinction is important, especially when assessed against the now-withdrawn DCB, which sought to define SSDEs based on quantitative data points, including revenue, user base, and geography.[31] Although the Bill is not yet law in India, it provides a useful insight into the government's thinking on competition regulation. It also indicates that Indian policymakers are increasingly considering a European Union (EU)-style (ex-ante) approach, where potential competition issues are addressed before they cause harm to the market.

In digital markets, data determines who holds market power under competition law, while under privacy law, it defines the limits of individual autonomy.[32] The two regimes, once considered distinct, now converge around this shared regulatory aspect. Digital markets do not rely on a fixed set of data; instead, they are structured around overlapping forms of data including personal information, behavioural data, location data, search and browsing histories, and transaction data.[33] A clearer understanding of how personal data and big data are used, both independently and in combination, is therefore essential to analysing data-driven market power.

The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) defines ‘personal data’ as any information that is or can be used to trace the natural person to which it belongs, or at least is capable of identifying that person through direct or indirect means, in particular “by reference to an identifier such as a name, location data, an identification number, an online identifier,” or any other characteristic, whether “physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural, or social.”[34] In the Indian context, the 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act defines ‘personal data’ as any data associated with an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to such data.[35]

In contrast, ‘big data’ is defined using five characteristics: “volume, velocity, variety, veracity and value.”[36] The European Commission (EC) defines it as “large amounts of different types of data produced from various types of sources, such as people, machines or sensors,” and includes “climate information, satellite imagery, digital pictures and videos, transition records, or GPS signals.”[37] The value of big data lies not only in collecting individual data points but in aggregating and analysing large-scale datasets. Every day, millions of users search, click links, use maps, watch videos, and browse websites. Some of this information is personal data, while much of it includes search trends, website traffic, and user interactions. When analysed together, these large datasets help improve search results, detect trends, personalise services, and support advertising. As such, personal data is a subset of big data, but it is often among its most valuable components as it can identify individual behaviours, preferences, and interactions.

Competition authorities increasingly recognise that exclusive access to large or unique datasets constitutes a barrier to entry and a source of dominance.[38] Dominant firms can leverage exclusive access to user data to create self-reinforcing cycles of power, to collect more data to improve services, attract more users, and thereby collect even more data.[39]

Technological advancements have enabled businesses to retain enormous amounts of data, use them to their advantage, and improve predictions, allowing for effective market interventions.[40] Gathering and storing data is as crucial as using it, as strategic application can give businesses an advantage over rivals.

Access to data can give firms a competitive advantage across multiple digital markets simultaneously. Companies that operate across different platforms and offer a range of products or services can combine data collected from these businesses to gain deeper insights into their users' preferences, behaviour, and needs. These insights can then be used to strengthen their position across markets.[41] Data typically serves as a “shareable input,” where information gathered through a particular good or service can be utilised to create new goods or enhance current ones, thus taking advantage of economies of scale.[42] Cross-market effects of this kind in several markets could lead to the development of interconnected digital ecosystems with high entry barriers and notable lock-in effects.

Google's acquisition of Fitbit in 2021 is a case in point. In addition to acquiring Fitbit's wearable technology, Google also gained access to a large repository of health and fitness data generated by millions of users, including information on physical activity, sleep patterns, and heart rate.[43] Even the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) had raised concerns that Google's access to this data could strengthen its existing data advantage, raise barriers to entry and further entrench its position in digital advertising and health markets.[44] Such datasets are valuable because they help firms improve existing products, develop new AI-powered services, and strengthen their position across interconnected digital markets. At the same time, the acquisition raised concerns about whether combining Fitbit's health data with Google's broader data ecosystem could further reinforce Google's market power while increasing its ability to collect and process personal information.[45]

Privacy is the hidden cost users pay for free online services,[46] collected through tracking behavioural and algorithmic profiling. Competitors without access to similar datasets face a disadvantage, strengthening established players and making it harder for new ones to compete. Consider the example of Amazon. Every time a customer searches for a product, makes a purchase, or leaves a review, the platform collects data. By analysing these millions of interactions together, Amazon can better understand customer preferences and recommend products that are more relevant to each user. [47]

Network effects amplify the competitive significance of data. The more users a platform attracts, the more personal data it accumulates. That data, in turn, enhances the quality of algorithms, services, and user experiences, drawing in more users in a self-reinforcing cycle.[48] This dynamic is particularly acute with personal data, as it enables platforms to refine personalisation and prediction, creating user lock-in and discouraging switching to rivals.[49] In such environments, markets can ‘tip’ rapidly in favour of a dominant player, making ex-post competition interventions slow and often ineffective. Unlike traditional network effects, where value grows linearly with users, data-driven network effects create exponential growth in competitive advantage.

For example, Google Search improves every time someone uses it; every search query and click provides Google with information about which results users find most relevant. As more people use the search engine, Google collects more data, enabling it to improve the quality and relevance of its search results. Better search results attract more users, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which increased usage leads to better services and further growth.[50]

Big Tech's competitive advantage is closely linked to its ability to collect and use large volumes of data. The more data a platform collects, the better it can improve its services, strengthen its market position, and attract more users. A 2022 survey of the five Big Tech firms—Facebook (now Meta), Google, Apple, Twitter (now X), and Amazon—reported that Google tracked 39 distinct data types per user, while Amazon tracked 23 and Facebook, 14.[51]

However, it is not just the volume of data that matters, but how different datasets are brought together. Combining data from multiple sources gives firms a stronger competitive advantage. Platforms combine account data, user location, multiple user profiles, behavioural telemetry (such as clicks, total time spent on sites, and browsing data), and third-party partner data to build durable user profiles that smaller firms cannot replicate.[52] These combined data sources can also be used to create detailed audience segments for targeted advertising, as platforms and advertisers draw on diverse data to build micro-segments of consumers and tailor advertisements to specific groups based on their interests and behavioural characteristics.[53] These practices are not only intrusive, but they also create competitive asymmetries.

AI intensifies this problem because it creates another way for personal data to enter systems without meaningful, informed consent, especially through web scraping[54] and downstream reuse[55] of datasets[a] for model training. This erosion of user consent expands the data resources of dominant platforms while smaller rivals lack such access, converting privacy violations into a source of competitive asymmetry in AI markets.

At the same time, public distrust in AI data usage has also worsened. According to the 2026 Stanford AI Index Report, global public nervousness about AI privacy and data usage reached 52 percent, while public confidence in institutions and firms to handle personal data responsibly remains strikingly low, with only 31 percent trusting government oversight in key markets.[56] At the same time, defensive measures against data harvesting have accelerated, with the proportion of web data explicitly blocked from AI scraper bots rising sharply to between 20 percent and 33 percent.[57]

In its 2025 Market Study on Artificial Intelligence and Competition, CCI recognised data as a key resource in AI markets.[58] It noted that data advantages, combined with network effects, tend to make markets more concentrated. Exclusive access to such data can therefore act as a barrier to entry, limiting opportunities for smaller firms.[59] Meanwhile, the constant drive to collect more data to improve AI models often weakens privacy protections through invasive tracking,[60] unclear consent,[61] or excessive data sharing.

As such, access to data determines the effectiveness and accuracy of AI systems.[62] Firms with large user bases collect more data than their competitors. When they use this data to train AI models, those models perform better and deliver more accurate results.[63] This improvement attracts even more users, who in turn generate more data. Over time, this creates a cycle of growing advantage for the firm. The more data it collects, the stronger its AI becomes, ultimately attracting even more data. As a result, data extraction forms a key competitive strategy for digital platforms and AI systems alike.

Viewed in this context, privacy becomes inseparable from competition law. Strong privacy constraints limit data accumulation and thus shape competitive outcomes. In this sense, privacy operates as a structural parameter of market competition rather than merely a right to autonomy.

Historically, privacy and competition laws were treated as distinct fields, but as markets have shifted to the digital domain, regulators have begun to recognise that how firms collect, process, and leverage personal data directly affects market dynamics.[64] Across jurisdictions, authorities are increasingly treating privacy as a parameter of competition, acknowledging that the degradation of privacy can be both a user harm and a source of dominance.[65]

The 2021 WhatsApp privacy dispute marked a turning point in Indian competition law. Acting suo motu, the CCI initiated an investigation into WhatsApp's updated privacy policy for alleged abuse of dominance under Section 4 of the 2002 Competition Act.[b],[66] The revised policy required users to compulsorily accept new terms permitting the sharing of their data with parent company Meta.[67] Continued use of the platform was conditional upon accepting these terms, leaving users with no meaningful choice.

The significance of the case lies in CCI's approach. Rather than treating the dispute solely as a question of privacy or data protection, the CCI examined whether a dominant platform could exploit its market position by imposing coercive data-sharing conditions on users.[68] WhatsApp and Meta challenged CCI's jurisdiction before the Delhi High Court, arguing that issues relating to privacy and consent fell exclusively within the domain of privacy and data protection law. A single-judge bench dismissed the petition,[69] allowing the CCI's investigation to proceed, a decision upheld on appeal by a two-judge bench.[70] Together, these decisions established that data practices may legitimately be examined through the lens of competition law where they raise concerns relating to market power and consumer harm.

In its final order in 2024,[71] CCI concluded that WhatsApp and Meta had abused their dominant position in violation of Sections 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(c), and 4(2)(e) of the 2002 Competition Act.[c] The CCI found that WhatsApp was dominant in the Indian market for OTT messaging applications through smartphones and that requiring users to share their data across the Meta ecosystem went beyond what was necessary to provide the messaging service. The CCI imposed an approximately US$22.3-million penalty, prohibited advertising-related data sharing for five years, and directed WhatsApp to introduce meaningful consent mechanisms for other categories of data sharing.[72] In doing so, the CCI recognised that exploitative data practices by a dominant digital platform could constitute an abuse of dominance, treating privacy as a non-price dimension of consumer welfare.

WhatsApp and Meta challenged the order before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), which substantially affirmed the CCI’s approach but refined its application. The tribunal upheld the penalty and confirmed the findings that WhatsApp had imposed unfair conditions on users and abused its dominant position. However, the NCLAT did not uphold CCI’s findings under Section 4(2)(e), or the accompanying five-year ban on sharing data for advertising purposes, holding that the evidence was insufficient to support those conclusions. More importantly, the NCLAT rejected WhatsApp's argument that privacy concerns fall exclusively within the scope of the Information Technology Act (2000) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023). Instead, it recognised that competition and data protection laws can work alongside each other. In other words, it was noted that a dominant company’s use of data can raise both competition and privacy concerns at the same time.[73]

Taken together, the decisions by the Delhi High Court, the CCI, and the NCLAT demonstrate an important doctrinal shift in Indian competition law. The NCLAT left intact the broader principle that data practices can amount to an abuse of dominance where they distort competition or undermine consumer choice. At the time of writing, the matter was pending before the Supreme Court of India, whose eventual decision will shape the future relationship between competition law and data protection in the country.

While the WhatsApp case demonstrates that privacy concerns are rampant in competition enforcement, the degree of integration between competition and data protection regimes varies across jurisdictions. Some jurisdictions maintain largely separate legal and institutional frameworks, while others have developed mechanisms for coordination, cross-regulatory consultation, or explicit recognition of privacy harms within competition analysis (see Table 1).
Largely disconnected. Data-driven market power is not structurally linked to privacy erosion; the linkage is left to courts and the CCI (for instance, in the WhatsApp case).

Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) collaborates with the Administrative Council for Economic Defense (CADE), Brazil’s competition authority; the Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD) (the data protection law) [77] informs the assessment of data-related competition concerns.
Competition Act 89 of 1998 (as amended in 2018)[78] treats data and platforms as central to economic inclusion and competition.
Conceptually aligned, institutionally separated. Data is recognised as economic power, but privacy law is not used as a competition lever.
Parallel regimes. Strong data protection exists, but it is not yet integrated into competition analysis of platform dominance.
Emerging convergence. Privacy is strong, but its role in disciplining digital market power remains underdeveloped.
High functional convergence. Competition and data regulators coordinate closely; data practices and algorithmic behaviour are explicitly considered in competition enforcement.
Digital Markets Act[86] imposes ex-ante obligations on gatekeepers, including limits on cross-service data combination, self-preferencing, and interoperability.
General Data Protection Regulation[87] governs consent, purpose limitation, profiling, and data subject rights.

Structurally integrated. The Digital Markets Act explicitly relies on General Data Protection Regulation consent standards to regulate how gatekeepers may combine and reuse personal data, making privacy a built-in competition control.

Antitrust laws in the US (Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890,[88] Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914,[89] Federal Trade Commission Act of 1914 (FTC Act)[90]) target monopolisation largely through litigation and settlements.
Siloed. Firms can resolve competition cases through payouts without surrendering data assets or AI-driven advantages.

Given growing concerns about data concentration and privacy degradation, jurisdictions worldwide have implemented ex-ante regulations to address perceived gaps in traditional enforcement. However, ex-ante regulation is best suited to situations where market failure occurs,[93] power is stable and entrenched, and the same firms occupy similar positions for long periods.[94]

The EU’s Digital Markets Act is an apt example of this regime, as it establishes upfront obligations for gatekeepers so their behaviour can be regulated; in doing so, it provides an alternative mechanism to restore contestability and fairness without requiring evidence of actual harm in every instance.[95]

India’s now-withdrawn Draft Digital Competition Bill attempted to adapt Digital Markets Act-style ex-ante regulation through the designation of SSDEs.[96] India’s decision to rely heavily on quantitative metrics such as turnover, user base, and market presence[97] signalled a move away from its historically effects-based and case-specific competition law tradition. By focusing on a firm’s identity rather than its behaviour, such an approach risked diluting the case-by-case analytical rigour that underpins competition enforcement.

The withdrawal of the Draft Digital Competition Bill illustrates the challenge in regulating dynamic technology markets with fixed thresholds. Though designed to curb data concentration and Big Tech dominance, the Bill never clearly demonstrated how proactive rules would protect competition and privacy any better than the existing antitrust framework.[98] The Bill also did not adequately show how privacy harm (often contextual, behavioural, and non-price based) would be evaluated in a status-driven regulatory regime.

In markets like India, where competition remains fluid and innovation is frequent, a case-by-case approach is better suited to identifying when data practices genuinely distort competition or undermine privacy, without presuming market failure in advance. India does not need a Digital Markets Act-style regime to discipline market structure; it needs institutional mechanisms to recognise when privacy degradation becomes a source of competitive advantage.

While competition authorities worldwide have increasingly acknowledged data privacy as a crucial aspect of competition law, drawing such a connection between the two does not necessarily provide a pragmatic solution to the problems associated with the digital economy. To be sure, cooperation among competition authorities and data protection regulators has improved the application of data protection laws such as the GDPR.[99] However, there is still insufficient evidence that such interaction will improve privacy standards while also addressing abuse of dominance by companies and intermediaries.[100]

The privacy paradox—the contradiction of people saying they are increasingly concerned about their online privacy yet are frequently using services that rely heavily on tracking their personal data, especially when such services are free or convenient—poses another challenge,[101],[102] as it stymies regulators’ efforts to frame privacy as a component of user harm under competition law. If users voluntarily share their data or accept terms that reduce privacy, it becomes difficult to argue that they are being harmed in a traditional competition sense. As a result, proving that certain data practices reduce user welfare is more complex, particularly when user choices appear to contradict their stated preferences.

Another challenge is the overlap between the two concepts across regulatory authorities. As authorities delve into both competition and data protection issues, the absence of a unified system can lead to conflicting rules and enforcement. Privacy harms, such as losing control over personal data, are harder to quantify and prove in court.[103] Indeed, trying to fit these intangible issues within competition law might dilute its primary focus on economic matters and shift it towards broader social issues.

To overcome antitrust challenges underlying the data privacy space, competition authorities will have to broaden their vision and tools to scrutinise anti-competitive effects. Given the dangers of concealed data practices and the privacy paradox, authorities need to understand users' preferences to determine whether they are aware of data protection measures in their market.

Globally, regulators are already experimenting with hybrid approaches: the EU’s Digital Markets Act establishes interoperability mandates that have privacy implications, while the UK and US are embedding privacy factors into competition analysis of AI markets. AI’s data dependency makes privacy and competition two sides of the same regulatory coin.

To develop contestability and innovation in its AI economy while also building trust requires India to move beyond siloed frameworks. Real-time detection of anti-competitive behaviour can be achieved with proactive monitoring tools. The practice of traditional ex-post enforcement would be of limited help to the regulator during the prevention of irreversible market tipping. There also needs to be a commitment to regularly changing/updating standards and norms. A regularly changing standard for dominance and norms governing data accumulation and consent may be required due to rapidly evolving AI tools. Transparency, improved consent dashboards, and accountability mechanisms will greatly enhance the quality of user choice, heighten user autonomy, and improve competition in digital marketplaces.

The withdrawal of the Draft Digital Competition Bill does not signify a lack of regulation, but a need to reassess and fine-tune the Indian government's response to competition in the data economy. Rather than defaulting to ex-ante designation, competition law can evolve to include privacy in its existing analytical framework. This would retain the flexibility of case-by-case enforcement, and allow regulators to examine the impact of data practices, consent structures, and obfuscatory privacy defaults on competition. This may not require a lot of new regulation. The lessons from the Digital Markets Act and the Draft Digital Competition Bill may draw India's Digital Market competition policy more closely linked to privacy. This would shift privacy's fundamental rights protective function to a more protective competitive function in the digital economy.

[a] Web scraping is an automated method of extracting large amounts of data from websites. This data, usually in HTML format, is converted into structured formats like spreadsheets or databases for further use. It can be done through online tools, APIs, or custom code. While major websites like Google, Twitter, and Facebook offer APIs for structured data access, web scraping is often used for sites that lack such options or restrict data access. Downstream reuse means taking personal data originally collected or posted online for one reason and using it to train or improve an AI system without the creator's or owner's permission.

[b] Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002, prohibits the abuse of dominant position, including the imposition of unfair conditions, denial of market access, and leveraging dominance from one market to another.

[c] According to the law, it is considered an abuse of dominant position if an enterprise or a group directly or indirectly, imposes unfair or discriminatory conditions in the purchase or sale of goods or services (Section 4(2)(a)(i)); indulges in practice or practices resulting in denial of market access in any manner (Section 4(2)(c));
or uses its dominant position in one relevant market to enter into, or protect, another relevant market (Section 4(2)(e)).
